report:
## Research Findings

The evidence strongly contradicts the premise that offering HIV self-testing (HIVST) does *not* increase testing uptake. Multiple systematic reviews and randomized controlled trials show the opposite: HIVST substantially **increases** the uptake of HIV testing.

A 2021 systematic review and meta-analysis in *eClinicalMedicine* (13 RCTs), which informed updated WHO guidance, found HIVST more than doubled testing uptake compared to standard testing services (RR: 2.09; 95% CI: 1.69–2.58; moderate-certainty evidence) (https://www.thelancet.com/journals/eclinm/article/PIIS2589-5370(21)00271-6/fulltext). A related meta-analysis published in the *Journal of the International AIDS Society* similarly concluded that "HIVST is associated with increased uptake and frequency of testing in RCTs" (https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.7448/IAS.20.1.21594). This body of work underpinned the WHO's 2016 recommendation endorsing self-testing as an effective strategy to reach populations, such as men and key populations, who might not otherwise test, and a subsequent WHO evidence update reaffirmed these findings (https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/WHO-CDS-HIV-19.36).

That said, the effect is not universal in every subgroup or setting. Some individual trials—particularly among populations already engaged in frequent testing, such as men who have sex with men in high-income settings, or specific occupational groups like Kenyan truck drivers—found no significant difference in uptake when self-testing was offered alongside an already-accessible rapid test option (e.g., a Kenyan RCT of truck drivers found no uptake difference between self-testing and supervised finger-prick testing).

**Conclusion:** The dominant, higher-quality evidence indicates the answer is "yes"—offering HIVST does increase testing uptake overall, especially among under-tested groups—though effects vary by population and comparator.
